source.text: וַיַּ֣רְא בִּלְעָ֗ם כִּ֣י ט֞וֹב בְּעֵינֵ֤י יְהוָה֙ לְבָרֵ֣ךְ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְלֹא־הָלַ֥ךְ כְּפַֽעַם־בְּפַ֖עַם לִקְרַ֣את נְחָשִׁ֑ים וַיָּ֥שֶׁת אֶל־הַמִּדְבָּ֖ר פָּנָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And saw Balaam that good [it was] in [the] eyes of Yahweh to bless Israel, and not he went as time by time to meet omens, and he set toward the wilderness his face.

en.L: And Balaam saw that it [was] good in the eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to bless Israel, and he did not go as time after time to meet omens, but he set his face toward the wilderness.
en.B: When Balaam saw that it pleased {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to bless Israel, he did not go off to look for omens as he had done the other times. Instead he turned his face toward the wilderness.
en.R: Balaam now saw that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was pleased to bless Israel. So he did not go off by himself to look for omens, as he had done the other times. Instead he turned and looked out toward the wilderness.

decisions.choice: omens: signs read by a diviner to learn what the gods intend
decisions.reason: Balaam was a hired diviner (22:7; Joshua 13:22). Before the first two oracles he went off alone to meet with God, perhaps also to watch for such signs (23:3, 15). The law forbids Israel to look for omens (Leviticus 19:26; Deuteronomy 18:10), and Balaam's second oracle had already said that no omen works against Jacob (23:23).

decisions.choice: as time by time: as on the other occasions
decisions.reason: The phrase means "as he had done each time before", looking back to the two earlier oracles (23:3-4, 15-16). This time he does not go aside at all.

decisions.choice: toward the wilderness: toward the plain where Israel was camped
decisions.reason: Israel was camped in the plains of Moab at the edge of the wilderness, east of the Jordan (22:1). Turning his face that way, Balaam looks straight at the people he was hired to curse (verse 2).

decisions.choice: it pleased the LORD / the LORD was pleased
decisions.reason: "Good in the eyes of" is a common way of saying that someone approves or is pleased. Balanced and Readable say it plainly; Literal keeps the picture.

source.text: וַיִּשָּׂ֨א בִלְעָ֜ם אֶת־עֵינָ֗יו וַיַּרְא֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל שֹׁכֵ֖ן לִשְׁבָטָ֑יו וַתְּהִ֥י עָלָ֖יו ר֥וּחַ אֱלֹהִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And lifted up Balaam his eyes and saw Israel dwelling by its tribes, and came on him [the] Spirit of God.

en.L: And Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw Israel camping by its tribes, and the Spirit of God came upon him.
en.B: Balaam looked up and saw Israel camped tribe by tribe, and the Spirit of God came upon him.
en.R: Balaam looked up and saw the people of Israel camped in their tribes. Then the Spirit of God came on him.

decisions.choice: camping by its tribes: the camp laid out in its ordered tribal divisions
decisions.reason: Israel camped in a fixed order, each tribe in its place around the tent of meeting (2:1-34). Balaam sees the whole ordered camp spread out below him, and the next oracle begins with the beauty of its tents (verse 5).

decisions.choice: the Spirit of God came upon him: God's Spirit took hold of him so that he spoke God's word
decisions.reason: Earlier the LORD "put a word in his mouth" (23:5, 16). Now the text says the Spirit of God came on him, as the Spirit came on the elders (11:25-26), on Saul (1 Samuel 10:10; 19:23) and on others whom God moved to speak. It says nothing in Balaam's favor: it is God who speaks through him, and Balaam is later remembered for leading Israel into sin (31:16).

decisions.choice: Spirit (capital S)
decisions.reason: The word can mean wind, breath or spirit. With "of God" and "came upon him" it is God's own Spirit at work, so it is capitalized, as elsewhere in these books.

source.text: וַיִּשָּׂ֥א מְשָׁל֖וֹ וַיֹּאמַ֑ר נְאֻ֤ם בִּלְעָם֙ בְּנ֣וֹ בְעֹ֔ר וּנְאֻ֥ם הַגֶּ֖בֶר שְׁתֻ֥ם הָעָֽיִן׃

records.literal_gloss: And he lifted up his oracle and said: utterance of Balaam son of Beor, and utterance of the man opened of the eye,

en.L: And he took up his oracle and said, \q "[The] utterance of Balaam son of Beor, \q and [the] utterance of the man whose eye [is] opened,
en.B: Then he spoke his oracle: \q "These are the words of Balaam son of Beor, \q the words of the man whose eye is opened,
en.R: Then he gave his message: \q "This is what Balaam son of Beor says, \q the man whose eye has been opened.

decisions.choice: took up his oracle: began to speak a solemn, poetic saying
decisions.reason: The word for oracle names a formal saying set in poetic lines: a proverb, a taunt song or, as here, a prophetic pronouncement (23:7, 18). To "lift it up" is to begin to speak it aloud.

decisions.choice: utterance: a solemn declaration that opens a prophetic word
decisions.reason: This word nearly always comes with God's name, in the phrase "the utterance of the LORD", which the prophets use to mark a message as his. Here and in verse 15 it is used with Balaam's own name, as it is for David's last words (2 Samuel 23:1) and for the sayings of Agur (Proverbs 30:1). Balaam presents himself as a seer speaking with authority.

decisions.choice: whose eye is opened: who sees what is hidden
alternatives: whose eye is closed (shut to ordinary sight, seeing in vision)
decisions.reason: The word for "opened" is found only here and in verse 15, so its sense is not certain. The parallel line in verse 4, "with eyes uncovered", supports "opened". A very similar word means "to stop up", and some read "whose eye is closed": shut to ordinary sight, but seeing in vision. Either way the line claims that Balaam sees what others cannot, which is pointed after the story of the donkey, where the LORD had to uncover his eyes before he could see the angel (22:31).

decisions.choice: These are the words of / This is what ... says
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the solemn opening formula does instead of using a word like "utterance", which is rare in everyday speech. Balanced uses "oracle" for the poem itself.

source.text: נְאֻ֕ם שֹׁמֵ֖עַ אִמְרֵי־אֵ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֨ר מַחֲזֵ֤ה שַׁדַּי֙ יֶֽחֱזֶ֔ה נֹפֵ֖ל וּגְל֥וּי עֵינָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: utterance of [one] hearing [the] words of God, who [the] vision of Shaddai sees, falling and uncovered of eyes:

en.L: [the] utterance of one who hears the words of God, \q who sees the vision of the Almighty, \q falling down, and [his] eyes uncovered:
en.B: the words of one who hears what God says, \q who sees the vision of the Almighty, \q who falls to the ground with eyes wide open:
en.R: He hears what God says. \q He sees the vision that God All-Powerful gives, \q falling to the ground with his eyes wide open.

decisions.choice: Shaddai: the Almighty
decisions.reason: Shaddai is an ancient title of God, used with the patriarchs (Genesis 17:1; 28:3; Exodus 6:3) and often in Job. Its origin is uncertain; it has long been understood as "the Almighty", the God who has power over all things.

decisions.choice: falling down, with eyes uncovered: overcome in a vision, yet seeing clearly
decisions.reason: Balaam is thrown to the ground, or bows down, as the vision comes on him, but his eyes are open to what God shows. The words echo 22:31, where the LORD uncovered Balaam's eyes, he saw the angel, and he bowed down with his face to the ground.

decisions.choice: God: the general word for God, here the God of Israel
decisions.reason: Balaam uses the short word for God, common in poetry, and in parallel with Shaddai. In his oracles it names the same God as the LORD (23:8, 19, 22-23).

decisions.choice: God All-Powerful
decisions.reason: Readable gives the title as "God All-Powerful", as elsewhere in Numbers to Ruth.

source.text: מַה־טֹּ֥בוּ אֹהָלֶ֖יךָ יַעֲקֹ֑ב מִשְׁכְּנֹתֶ֖יךָ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: How good are your tents, Jacob, your dwellings, Israel!

en.L: How good are your tents, Jacob, \q your dwellings, Israel!
en.B: How fine your tents are, Jacob, \q your dwellings, Israel!
en.R: Jacob, your tents are so beautiful! \q Israel, your homes are so lovely!

decisions.choice: how good: how fine and fair
decisions.reason: The word means good to look at and good to live in: lovely, prosperous, well ordered. It picks up verse 1, where it was "good in the eyes of the LORD" to bless Israel.

decisions.choice: dwellings: the people's homes, here their tents
decisions.reason: The word is the plural of the word used for the tabernacle, but here, in parallel with "tents", it means the places where the people live.

decisions.choice: Jacob ... Israel: two names for the one people, addressed directly
decisions.reason: As in the earlier oracles (23:7, 10, 21, 23), the two names stand side by side in parallel lines. Balaam now speaks to Israel itself.

decisions.choice: Jacob, your tents are so beautiful! / Israel, your homes are so lovely!
decisions.reason: Readable puts the names first and makes each line a full sentence, so the exclamation is easy to follow.

source.text: כִּנְחָלִ֣ים נִטָּ֔יוּ כְּגַנֹּ֖ת עֲלֵ֣י נָהָ֑ר כַּאֲהָלִים֙ נָטַ֣ע יְהוָ֔ה כַּאֲרָזִ֖ים עֲלֵי־מָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: Like valleys [that] stretch out, like gardens beside a river, like aloes [that] planted Yahweh, like cedars beside waters.

en.L: Like valleys [that] stretch out, \q like gardens beside a river, \q like aloes [that] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has planted, \q like cedars beside waters.
en.B: They are like stream valleys reaching far, \q like gardens by a river, \q like aloes that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has planted, \q like cedars beside the water.
en.R: They stretch out like valleys with streams, like gardens by a river. \q They are like sweet-smelling aloe trees that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has planted, like cedars growing by the water.

decisions.choice: valleys that stretch out: long valleys with streams running through them
decisions.reason: The word names a valley cut by a stream that may run only in the rainy season. Some take it here as a word for groves of palms, to match the plants in the next lines, but the usual sense fits the picture of water that runs through the whole verse.

decisions.choice: aloes: fragrant trees
decisions.reason: Aloes here are trees prized for their fragrant wood (Psalm 45:9; Proverbs 7:17; Song 4:14), not the desert plant now called aloe. The word sounds almost the same as "your tents" in verse 5, a play on words that ties the two verses together. The poem is not describing a real orchard: it heaps up pictures of rich, well-watered growth.

decisions.choice: that the LORD has planted: Israel's flourishing is the LORD's work
decisions.reason: Israel is pictured as a plantation the LORD himself has set out, as in Exodus 15:17 and Psalm 80:9-12, where God plants his people in their land.

decisions.choice: They are like ... / They stretch out like ...
decisions.reason: The Hebrew lines are a string of comparisons with no verb. Balanced and Readable supply "they are", meaning Israel's tents and camps.

decisions.choice: sweet-smelling aloe trees
decisions.reason: Readable says what aloes are, since readers know the word only as a desert plant.

source.text: יִֽזַּל־מַ֨יִם֙ מִדָּ֣לְיָ֔ו וְזַרְע֖וֹ בְּמַ֣יִם רַבִּ֑ים וְיָרֹ֤ם מֵֽאֲגַג֙ מַלְכּ֔וֹ וְתִנַּשֵּׂ֖א מַלְכֻתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Will flow water from his buckets, and his seed [will be] in many waters; and will be higher than Agag his king, and will be exalted his kingdom.

en.L: Water will flow from his buckets, \q and his seed [will be] in many waters; \q and his king will be higher than Agag, \q and his kingdom will be exalted.
en.B: Water will flow from his buckets, \q and his seed will have abundant water. \q His king will be greater than Agag, \q and his kingdom will be lifted high.
en.R: They will have water to spare, \q and the seed they plant will have plenty of water. \q Their king will be greater than King Agag, \q and their kingdom will be honored.

decisions.choice: water flowing from his buckets: water in abundance
decisions.reason: Israel is pictured as a man whose water buckets overflow. In a dry land, plenty of water means life and good harvests.

decisions.choice: his seed: the seed sown in his fields, with a hint at his descendants
decisions.reason: In a verse about water the first sense is seed planted in well-watered ground. The same word also means offspring, and the next lines turn to Israel's king and kingdom, so the line may also promise that Israel's children will thrive.

decisions.choice: Agag: the Hebrew text's reading
decisions.reason: Agag was the name, or perhaps the royal title, of the kings of Amalek (1 Samuel 15:8-9, 32-33), the nation Balaam speaks of in verse 20. The ancient Greek translation reads "Gog" here, and its version of this verse differs in other ways too, speaking of a man who will come from Israel's seed and rule many nations. The Hebrew text is followed. Reviewers should check this against a textual apparatus.

decisions.choice: his king, his kingdom: a king for Israel in the future
decisions.reason: Israel had no king when these words were spoken. The oracle looks ahead to a kingdom among Israel's descendants, as God promised Abraham and Jacob that kings would come from them (Genesis 17:6; 35:11). Verse 17 takes the theme further.

decisions.choice: they / their
decisions.reason: The poem speaks of Israel as one man, "he". Readable uses "they" for the people throughout the oracle.

source.text: אֵ֚ל מוֹצִיא֣וֹ מִמִּצְרַ֔יִם כְּתוֹעֲפֹ֥ת רְאֵ֖ם ל֑וֹ יֹאכַ֞ל גּוֹיִ֣ם צָרָ֗יו וְעַצְמֹתֵיהֶ֛ם יְגָרֵ֖ם וְחִצָּ֥יו יִמְחָֽץ׃

records.literal_gloss: God [is] bringing him out from Egypt; like [the] horns of a wild ox [are] to him; he will devour nations, his foes, and their bones he will break, and his arrows he will strike.

en.L: God [is] bringing him out of Egypt; \q like the horns of a wild ox [are] his. \q He will devour nations, his foes, and he will break their bones, and [with] his arrows he will strike [them].
en.B: God brings him out of Egypt; \q his strength is like the horns of a wild ox. \q He will devour the nations that are his enemies, crush their bones and strike them with his arrows.
en.R: God is the one who brings them out of Egypt. \q They are as strong as a wild ox. \q They will swallow up the nations that fight against them, break their bones and shoot them down with arrows.

decisions.choice: a repeated line: the first half of the verse repeats 23:22
decisions.reason: The words are those of the second oracle (23:22), except that "bringing them" becomes "bringing him". The God who brought Israel out of Egypt is the source of its strength.

decisions.choice: like the horns of a wild ox: strength that cannot be tamed
decisions.reason: The wild ox, the great wild bull of the ancient world, was known for its strength and could not be tamed (Job 39:9-12). Its horns stand for power (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 92:11). The word for "horns" is rare and may mean peaks or great strength; the picture is the same.

decisions.choice: his: the strength belongs to Israel, given by God
decisions.reason: Since the next line goes on with Israel devouring nations, "his" most likely refers to Israel, who has the strength of a wild ox because God brought him out. It could also mean that God is like a wild ox's horns for Israel.

decisions.choice: he will strike them with his arrows
alternatives: he will crush their loins (a slightly different reading of one word)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "and his arrows he will strike". It most likely means that Israel will strike his enemies with his arrows. Some read "he will shatter their arrows", and some take one word, by a small change, as "their loins".

decisions.choice: them / they / their
decisions.reason: As in verse 7, Readable uses "they" for Israel, whom the poem calls "he".

source.text: כָּרַ֨ע שָׁכַ֧ב כַּאֲרִ֛י וּכְלָבִ֖יא מִ֣י יְקִימֶ֑נּוּ מְבָרֲכֶ֣יךָ בָר֔וּךְ וְאֹרְרֶ֖יךָ אָרֽוּר׃

records.literal_gloss: He crouched, he lay down like a lion, and like a lioness; who will rouse him? Those blessing you [are] blessed, and those cursing you [are] cursed.

en.L: He crouched, he lay down like a lion, and like a lioness; who will rouse him? \q Those who bless you [are] blessed, \q and those who curse you [are] cursed."
en.B: He crouches and lies down like a lion, like a lioness: who dares to rouse him? \q Blessed are those who bless you, \q and cursed are those who curse you!"
en.R: Israel is like a lion lying down to rest. Who would dare to wake it? \q Everyone who blesses you will be blessed, \q and everyone who curses you will be cursed."

decisions.choice: the lion that no one dares to rouse: Jacob's blessing of Judah
decisions.reason: These words almost repeat Jacob's blessing of Judah (Genesis 49:9), and they carry on the lion picture of 23:24. The lion has made its kill and lies at rest; no one would be foolish enough to disturb it.

decisions.choice: blessed are those who bless you: God's promise to Abraham and Isaac's blessing of Jacob
decisions.reason: The last two lines repeat Isaac's blessing of Jacob (Genesis 27:29) and echo God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3). Balak had sent for Balaam because "whoever you bless is blessed, and whoever you curse is cursed" (22:6). Now Balaam says that it is the way people treat Israel that brings blessing or curse on them, and Balak, who wants Israel cursed, stands under that word.

decisions.choice: lioness: a second word for a lion
decisions.reason: Hebrew poetry often pairs two words for one animal. The second word may mean a lioness or simply a lion; the pair stresses the picture rather than adding a second animal.

decisions.choice: Israel is like a lion lying down to rest
decisions.reason: Readable names Israel and says that the lion lies at rest, so the picture is clear. It uses "it" for the lion.

source.text: וַיִּֽחַר־אַ֤ף בָּלָק֙ אֶל־בִּלְעָ֔ם וַיִּסְפֹּ֖ק אֶת־כַּפָּ֑יו וַיֹּ֨אמֶר בָּלָ֜ק אֶל־בִּלְעָ֗ם לָקֹ֤ב אֹֽיְבַי֙ קְרָאתִ֔יךָ וְהִנֵּה֙ בֵּרַ֣כְתָּ בָרֵ֔ךְ זֶ֖ה שָׁלֹ֥שׁ פְּעָמִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And burned [the] anger of Balak against Balaam, and he struck his palms, and said Balak to Balaam: to curse my enemies I called you, and here, you have blessed [them] a blessing these three times.

en.L: And the anger of Balak burned against Balaam, and he struck his hands together. And Balak said to Balaam, "I called you to curse my enemies, and look, you have done nothing but bless [them] these three times.
en.B: Balak was furious with Balaam. He struck his hands together and said to Balaam, "I called you here to curse my enemies, and instead you have done nothing but bless them, three times now.
en.R: Balak became very angry with Balaam. He clapped his hands in anger and said, "I brought you here to put a curse on my enemies. But you have blessed them, not once but three times!

decisions.choice: struck his hands together: a gesture of anger and contempt
decisions.reason: Clapping or striking the hands could show scorn and fury (Job 27:23; Lamentations 2:15). Balak is enraged and shows contempt for the seer who has failed him.

decisions.choice: you have done nothing but bless them
decisions.reason: The verb "bless" is doubled, a Hebrew way of stressing an action. Balak means that instead of cursing, Balaam has blessed Israel outright, and done so three times (23:7-10, 18-24; 24:3-9).

decisions.choice: his anger burned: he became very angry
decisions.reason: The same picture is used of the LORD's anger against Balaam in 22:22.

decisions.choice: clapped his hands in anger
decisions.reason: Readable adds "in anger" so that the gesture is not read as applause.

source.text: וְעַתָּ֖ה בְּרַח־לְךָ֣ אֶל־מְקוֹמֶ֑ךָ אָמַ֨רְתִּי֙ כַּבֵּ֣ד אֲכַבֶּדְךָ֔ וְהִנֵּ֛ה מְנָעֲךָ֥ יְהוָ֖ה מִכָּבֽוֹד׃

records.literal_gloss: And now flee for yourself to your place. I said, honoring I will honor you, and here, has held back you Yahweh from honor.

en.L: So now flee to your place. I said, 'I will greatly honor you,' and look, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has held you back from honor."
en.B: Now get out of here and go home! I said I would reward you with great honor, but {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has kept you from any honor."
en.R: Now hurry back home! I promised to reward you and make you a great man. But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has kept you from getting any reward."

decisions.choice: honor: honor shown by rich payment and favor
decisions.reason: Balak's first message promised to honor Balaam greatly (22:17, 37), meaning rewards and gifts as well as respect. Now he says the reward is lost.

decisions.choice: flee to your place: leave at once and go home
decisions.reason: Balak dismisses Balaam in anger. "Your place" is Balaam's home country (22:5).

decisions.choice: the LORD has held you back: Balak blames the LORD
decisions.reason: Balak sees that the LORD is behind Balaam's blessings, which is what Balaam has said all along (22:18; 23:12, 26). Without meaning to, the king admits that Israel's God is in control.

decisions.choice: reward you with great honor / reward you
decisions.reason: "Honor" here includes payment. Balanced joins the two ideas; Readable says it as a reward that would make him a great man.

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר בִּלְעָ֖ם אֶל־בָּלָ֑ק הֲלֹ֗א גַּ֧ם אֶל־מַלְאָכֶ֛יךָ אֲשֶׁר־שָׁלַ֥חְתָּ אֵלַ֖י דִּבַּ֥רְתִּי לֵאמֹֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Balaam to Balak: [did] not also to your messengers whom you sent to me I speak, saying,

en.L: And Balaam said to Balak, "Did I not also speak to your messengers whom you sent to me, saying,
en.B: Balaam answered Balak, "Did I not tell the messengers you sent to me,
en.R: Balaam answered Balak, "I told the messengers you sent to me exactly this:

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer yes
decisions.reason: Balaam reminds Balak of what he said at the start (22:18): he warned the messengers then that he could say only what the LORD told him.

decisions.choice: I told ... exactly this
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into a plain statement, which says the same thing more simply.

source.text: אִם־יִתֶּן־לִ֨י בָלָ֜ק מְלֹ֣א בֵיתוֹ֮ כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָב֒ לֹ֣א אוּכַ֗ל לַעֲבֹר֙ אֶת־פִּ֣י יְהוָ֔ה לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת טוֹבָ֛ה א֥וֹ רָעָ֖ה מִלִּבִּ֑י אֲשֶׁר־יְדַבֵּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֹת֥וֹ אֲדַבֵּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: If gives to me Balak [the] fullness of his house [of] silver and gold, not I am able to go beyond [the] mouth of Yahweh to do good or bad from my heart; what speaks Yahweh, it I will speak?

en.L: 'If Balak gave me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go beyond the mouth of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, to do good or bad from my own heart; what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} speaks, that I will speak'?
en.B: 'Even if Balak gave me his house filled with silver and gold, I could not go beyond the command of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to do anything good or bad of my own will. What {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says, that is what I will say'?
en.R: 'Even if Balak gave me his house full of silver and gold, I could not go against what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} commands. I could not do anything at all, good or bad, on my own. I will say only what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} tells me.'

decisions.choice: a repeated answer: Balaam's first reply to Balak's messengers
decisions.reason: Balaam quotes almost word for word what he told Balak's officials in 22:18, adding "good or bad, from my own heart". The house full of silver and gold stands for the largest payment Balak could offer.

decisions.choice: go beyond the mouth of the LORD: disobey what the LORD has said
decisions.reason: "The mouth of the LORD" means what he commands (as in 9:18, 20; 22:18). To "go beyond" it is to overstep it.

decisions.choice: good or bad from my own heart: anything at all on my own initiative
decisions.reason: "Good or bad" pairs opposites to mean anything whatever (Genesis 24:50; 31:24). "From my heart" means by his own choice; Moses uses the same phrase in 16:28.

decisions.choice: the command of the LORD / what the LORD commands
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "mouth"; Balanced and Readable say what it means.

source.text: וְעַתָּ֕ה הִנְנִ֥י הוֹלֵ֖ךְ לְעַמִּ֑י לְכָה֙ אִיעָ֣צְךָ֔ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יַעֲשֶׂ֜ה הָעָ֥ם הַזֶּ֛ה לְעַמְּךָ֖ בְּאַחֲרִ֥ית הַיָּמִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And now, here I [am] going to my people. Come, I will advise you [of] what will do this people to your people in [the] end of the days.

en.L: And now, look, I [am] going to my people. Come, I will advise you [of] what this people will do to your people in the latter days."
en.B: So now I am going back to my people. But come, let me tell you what this people will do to your people in the days to come."
en.R: Now I am going home to my own people. But first, let me tell you what Israel will do to your people in the future."

decisions.choice: in the latter days: in the time ahead
decisions.reason: The phrase means the later part of the days, the future that lies ahead, sometimes far ahead (Genesis 49:1; Deuteronomy 4:30; 31:29). It does not by itself mean the end of the world. Here it points to the time when Israel will be settled and ruled by a king (verses 17-19).

decisions.choice: advise you: tell you, give you knowledge
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to give counsel. Here it introduces a prediction: Balaam will let Balak know what is coming. Numbers 31:16 speaks of a different piece of advice from Balaam, which led Israel into sin at Peor (chapter 25).

decisions.choice: this people ... your people: Israel and Moab
decisions.reason: "This people" is Israel, camped before them; "your people" is Balak's nation, Moab, which verse 17 names.

decisions.choice: Israel
decisions.reason: Readable names Israel instead of saying "this people".

source.text: וַיִּשָּׂ֥א מְשָׁל֖וֹ וַיֹּאמַ֑ר נְאֻ֤ם בִּלְעָם֙ בְּנ֣וֹ בְעֹ֔ר וּנְאֻ֥ם הַגֶּ֖בֶר שְׁתֻ֥ם הָעָֽיִן׃

records.literal_gloss: And he lifted up his oracle and said: utterance of Balaam son of Beor, and utterance of the man opened of the eye,

en.L: And he took up his oracle and said, \q "[The] utterance of Balaam son of Beor, \q and [the] utterance of the man whose eye [is] opened,
en.B: Then he spoke his oracle: \q "These are the words of Balaam son of Beor, \q the words of the man whose eye is opened,
en.R: Then Balaam gave his message: \q "This is what Balaam son of Beor says, \q the man whose eye has been opened.

decisions.choice: the opening of the fourth oracle repeats verse 3
decisions.reason: The words are the same as in verse 3; see the decisions there on "utterance" and on the uncertain word "opened". This last oracle is given without Balak asking for it (verse 14).

decisions.choice: As in verse 3.
decisions.reason: The same wording is used as in verse 3, so the two openings match.

source.text: נְאֻ֗ם שֹׁמֵ֨עַ֙ אִמְרֵי־אֵ֔ל וְיֹדֵ֖עַ דַּ֣עַת עֶלְי֑וֹן מַחֲזֵ֤ה שַׁדַּי֙ יֶֽחֱזֶ֔ה נֹפֵ֖ל וּגְל֥וּי עֵינָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: utterance of [one] hearing [the] words of God, and knowing [the] knowledge of [the] Most High, [the] vision of Shaddai he sees, falling and uncovered of eyes:

en.L: [the] utterance of one who hears the words of God \q and knows the knowledge of the Most High, \q [who] sees the vision of the Almighty, \q falling down, and [his] eyes uncovered:
en.B: the words of one who hears what God says \q and has knowledge from the Most High, \q who sees the vision of the Almighty, \q who falls to the ground with eyes wide open:
en.R: He hears what God says. \q He has been given knowledge by the Most High God. \q He sees the vision that God All-Powerful gives, \q falling to the ground with his eyes wide open.

decisions.choice: the Most High
decisions.reason: A title of God as the one above all (Genesis 14:18-22; Deuteronomy 32:8). It stands here beside "God" and "Shaddai", three names for the one God.

decisions.choice: the knowledge of the Most High: knowledge that comes from him
decisions.reason: This line is the one addition to the opening of verses 3-4. It means that Balaam knows what the Most High makes known to him, not that he knows all that God knows.

decisions.choice: the rest of the verse repeats verse 4
decisions.reason: See the decisions at verse 4 on Shaddai and on "falling down, with eyes uncovered".

decisions.choice: the Most High God
decisions.reason: Readable adds "God" so that the title is clearly a name for God.

source.text: אֶרְאֶ֨נּוּ֙ וְלֹ֣א עַתָּ֔ה אֲשׁוּרֶ֖נּוּ וְלֹ֣א קָר֑וֹב דָּרַ֨ךְ כּוֹכָ֜ב מִֽיַּעֲקֹ֗ב וְקָ֥ם שֵׁ֨בֶט֙ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וּמָחַץ֙ פַּאֲתֵ֣י מוֹאָ֔ב וְקַרְקַ֖ר כָּל־בְּנֵי־שֵֽׁת׃

records.literal_gloss: I see him, and not now; I observe him, and not near. Has marched a star from Jacob, and will rise a scepter from Israel, and he will crush [the] two sides of Moab, and tear down all [the] sons of Sheth.

en.L: I see him, but not now; \q I observe him, but not near. \q A star will march out from Jacob, and a scepter will rise from Israel, \q and he will crush the temples [of the head] of Moab \q and tear down all the {{gender:children|sons}} of Sheth.
en.B: I see him, but not now; \q I look on him, but he is not near. \q A star will march out of Jacob, and a scepter will rise from Israel; \q he will crush the forehead of Moab \q and tear down all the {{gender:people|sons}} of Sheth.
en.R: I see someone, but not now. \q I look at him, but he is not near. \q A star will come from Jacob's people, and a ruler holding a scepter will rise up from Israel. \q He will crush Moab's head \q and destroy all the {{gender:people|sons}} of Sheth.

decisions.choice: I see him ... not near: a figure far in the future
decisions.reason: "Him" is the one the next lines describe, the star and scepter. Balaam sees him in vision but says plainly that he belongs to a time still distant, "the latter days" of verse 14. The verbs that follow speak of that future: the first is a form Hebrew prophecy uses to describe a coming event as if it had already happened.

decisions.choice: a star will march out from Jacob: a king will arise from Israel
decisions.reason: A star was a common picture for a king in the ancient world, and Scripture also uses it of rulers (Isaiah 14:12). The parallel line, with its scepter, makes the meaning clear: the star is a royal ruler. The verb means to tread or set out on the march, as a star moves on its course and as an army marches out.

decisions.choice: a scepter will rise from Israel: royal rule, as in Jacob's blessing of Judah
decisions.reason: The scepter is a king's rod of office. The same word means "tribe" (verse 2), but here, in parallel with "star", it means a ruler. The line echoes Genesis 49:10, "the scepter will not depart from Judah", which verse 9 has already recalled.

decisions.choice: the oracle's first fulfillment: David's victories over Moab and Edom
decisions.reason: Israel's king who first conquered Moab and Edom was David (2 Samuel 8:2, 13-14), and this is the kind of king the oracle describes: a ruler from Israel who crushes Moab (verse 17) and takes Edom (verse 18).

decisions.choice: the star and scepter came to be read as the promised Messiah
decisions.reason: The verse itself speaks of a future king from Israel who will defeat Moab and Edom. In later times Jews and Christians read it as pointing to the Messiah. Ancient Aramaic translations of the Torah render the scepter as the Messiah. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Damascus Document applies the star and the scepter to leaders expected in the last days. In AD 132-135, Simon bar Kosiba, who led the second Jewish revolt against Rome, was called Bar Kokhba, "son of the star", in the light of it. Christian readers have linked it with the star that led the wise men to the newborn king of the Jews (Matthew 2:2) and with Jesus as "the bright morning star" (Revelation 22:16), though neither passage quotes this verse. These later readings are part of the verse's history; they are not stated in the oracle itself.

decisions.choice: crush the temples of Moab: strike Moab's head, a death blow
decisions.reason: The word means the two sides, here the sides of the head. Moab is pictured as a warrior struck on the head. Jeremiah 48:45 takes up this line, saying that fire will consume "the forehead of Moab".

decisions.choice: tear down: the Hebrew text's verb
alternatives: and the skull of all the sons of Sheth
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has a verb meaning to tear down or break down. Jeremiah 48:45, which reuses the line, has a very similar word meaning "the crown of the head", and the Samaritan form of the Pentateuch is reported to read that word here, giving "the forehead of Moab and the skull of all the sons of Sheth". The meaning is much the same either way. Reviewers should check the Samaritan reading against a textual apparatus.

decisions.choice: the sons of Sheth: a people near Moab, of uncertain identity
decisions.reason: In parallel with Moab, the name most likely means a people of the region. Sheth is spelled like Seth, the son of Adam (Genesis 4:25), and some read "all the sons of Seth" as all humankind, but that sits poorly beside Moab. Others connect it with a nomad people known from Egyptian records of the area. Jeremiah 48:45, which echoes this line, has "the sons of tumult" instead, which may be the way that prophet understood the name.

decisions.choice: march out
decisions.reason: "Will march out" keeps the movement in the verb and its sense of an army setting out. The more familiar "come out" loses that.

decisions.choice: a ruler holding a scepter
decisions.reason: Readable names the ruler who holds the scepter, so the picture is understood. The star is kept, and its meaning is in the decisions.

decisions.choice: children / people of Sheth
decisions.reason: "Sons of" here names a whole people, men and women, so the gender setting gives "children" or "people" by default and "sons" as the alternative.

source.text: וְהָיָ֨ה אֱד֜וֹם יְרֵשָׁ֗ה וְהָיָ֧ה יְרֵשָׁ֛ה שֵׂעִ֖יר אֹיְבָ֑יו וְיִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל עֹ֥שֶׂה חָֽיִל׃

records.literal_gloss: And will be Edom a possession, and will be a possession Seir, his enemies; and Israel [is] doing strength.

en.L: And Edom will be a possession, and Seir, his enemies, will be a possession; \q and Israel does valiantly.
en.B: Edom will become his possession; Seir, his enemies, will become his possession, \q while Israel does mighty deeds.
en.R: He will take over Edom, the land of Seir, the land of his enemies. \q And Israel will grow strong.

decisions.choice: Edom and Seir: one nation, named by its people and by its hill country
decisions.reason: Seir is the mountain country where Edom, the descendants of Esau, lived (Genesis 32:4; 36:8-9). Edom had refused to let Israel pass through its land (20:14-21).

decisions.choice: a possession ... his enemies: conquered land that belongs to the ruler of verse 17
decisions.reason: "His enemies" stands beside Seir and describes it: Edom and Seir, though they are his enemies, will become the property of the coming ruler. The word for possession is used of land taken by conquest. David put garrisons in Edom and made it subject to him (2 Samuel 8:13-14).

decisions.choice: doing strength: acting with power and growing strong
decisions.reason: The phrase means to act bravely in battle and so to prosper (Psalm 60:14; 118:15). In other places it means to gain wealth (Deuteronomy 8:17-18); here, after conquest, the sense of power is closer.

decisions.choice: his possession / he will take over
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whose possession Edom becomes, the ruler of verse 17, as the grammar decision explains.

source.text: וְיֵ֖רְדְּ מִֽיַּעֲקֹ֑ב וְהֶֽאֱבִ֥יד שָׂרִ֖יד מֵעִֽיר׃

records.literal_gloss: And will rule [one] from Jacob, and will destroy [the] survivor from [the] city.

en.L: And one from Jacob will rule, \q and he will destroy the survivor from [the] city."
en.B: One from Jacob will rule, \q and he will wipe out the survivors of the city."
en.R: A ruler will come from Jacob's people. \q He will destroy those who are left in the city."

decisions.choice: one from Jacob will rule: the ruler of verse 17
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject: the one who rules is the one "from Jacob", the star and scepter of verse 17. The form of the verb can also be read as a wish ("may one from Jacob rule"), but in this run of predictions it says what will happen.

decisions.choice: the city: an enemy city, not named
alternatives: Ar, the chief city of Moab
decisions.reason: The verse does not say which city. It may mean the cities of Edom and Moab in general, or a particular stronghold, such as Ar, the city of Moab (21:15, 28; 22:36). The point is that none of the enemy who flee to a city will escape.

decisions.choice: A ruler will come from Jacob's people
decisions.reason: Readable names the subject as a ruler, as the grammar decision explains, and keeps the two short lines.

source.text: וַיַּרְא֙ אֶת־עֲמָלֵ֔ק וַיִּשָּׂ֥א מְשָׁל֖וֹ וַיֹּאמַ֑ר רֵאשִׁ֤ית גּוֹיִם֙ עֲמָלֵ֔ק וְאַחֲרִית֖וֹ עֲדֵ֥י אֹבֵֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And he saw Amalek, and he lifted up his oracle and said: first of [the] nations [was] Amalek, and his end [is] to destruction.

en.L: And he saw Amalek, and he took up his oracle and said, \q "Amalek [was] the first of the nations, \q but his end [will be] destruction."
en.B: Then he looked at Amalek and spoke his oracle: \q "Amalek was first among the nations, \q but in the end it will perish completely."
en.R: Then Balaam looked toward the Amalekites and said: \q "Amalek was the first of the nations, \q but in the end it will be completely destroyed."

decisions.choice: the first of the nations: the first to attack Israel, and proud of its rank
alternatives: the foremost or chief of the nations
decisions.reason: Amalek was the first nation to make war on Israel after the escape from Egypt (Exodus 17:8-16). The phrase can also mean the foremost of the nations (Amos 6:1 uses it of Israel's proud leaders), and both senses may be heard: Amalek counts itself first, but its end is ruin.

decisions.choice: his end will be destruction: the LORD's sentence on Amalek
decisions.reason: "First" and "end" are set against each other. After Amalek attacked Israel, the LORD said he would blot out the memory of Amalek (Exodus 17:14; Deuteronomy 25:17-19), and Saul and David later fought them (1 Samuel 15; 30).

decisions.choice: he saw Amalek: he looked toward the Amalekites' land, or saw them in vision
decisions.reason: Amalek lived in the southern wilderness, far from the hill where Balaam stood. He may have looked out in their direction, or seen them in the vision given to him; the text does not say which.

decisions.choice: it will perish completely / it will be completely destroyed
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "until destruction", meaning ruin that leaves nothing. Balanced and Readable use "it" for the nation.

source.text: וַיַּרְא֙ אֶת־הַקֵּינִ֔י וַיִּשָּׂ֥א מְשָׁל֖וֹ וַיֹּאמַ֑ר אֵיתָן֙ מֽוֹשָׁבֶ֔ךָ וְשִׂ֥ים בַּסֶּ֖לַע קִנֶּֽךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he saw the Kenite, and he lifted up his oracle and said: enduring [is] your dwelling place, and set in the rock [is] your nest,

en.L: And he saw the Kenites, and he took up his oracle and said, \q "Your dwelling place [is] enduring, \q and your nest [is] set in the rock,
en.B: Then he looked at the Kenites and spoke his oracle: \q "Your home is secure, \q and your nest is set in the rock,
en.R: Then Balaam looked at the Kenites and said: \q "Your home is safe and strong. \q You have built your nest high in the rocks.

decisions.choice: the Kenites: a clan living among and beside Israel
decisions.reason: The Kenites were a clan related to Moses' father-in-law (Judges 1:16; 4:11). Some of them lived near the Amalekites in the south (1 Samuel 15:6), which may be why this oracle follows the one on Amalek.

decisions.choice: your nest set in the rock: a home that seems out of reach
decisions.reason: The picture is of an eagle's nest on a high cliff, a place no enemy could reach (Jeremiah 49:16; Obadiah 4). The word for nest sounds like Kain, the name of the Kenite people (verse 22), a play on words.

decisions.choice: enduring: lasting and firm
decisions.reason: The word describes what is permanent and strong, like a stream that never runs dry. The Kenites' home looks secure, which makes the turn in verse 22 all the sharper.

decisions.choice: You have built your nest high in the rocks
decisions.reason: Readable makes the Kenites the subject of the second line so that it reads as a plain sentence.

source.text: כִּ֥י אִם־יִהְיֶ֖ה לְבָ֣עֵֽר קָ֑יִן עַד־מָ֖ה אַשּׁ֥וּר תִּשְׁבֶּֽךָּ׃

records.literal_gloss: nevertheless will be for burning Kain; until what? Asshur will take you captive.

en.L: nevertheless Kain will be for burning. \q How long until Asshur takes you captive?"
en.B: yet Kain will be burned up. \q How long until Asshur carries you away captive?"
en.R: But the people of Kain will be destroyed. \q How long will it be until Assyria takes you away as prisoners?"

decisions.choice: nevertheless: in spite of your secure home
decisions.reason: The two small words together mean "but yet" or "nevertheless", turning from the safety of verse 21 to the coming ruin.

decisions.choice: Kain will be for burning: the Kenites will be destroyed
decisions.reason: Kain is the name of the Kenite people as a whole, after their ancestor (Judges 4:11). "For burning" means given over to be consumed by fire, that is, destroyed.

decisions.choice: how long until: the end will come, though not at once
alternatives: How long? Asshur will take you captive (the question standing on its own)
decisions.reason: The words mean "until what?" or "how long?". Read with the rest of the line, they ask how long it will be before Asshur takes the Kenites captive: their ruin is sure, though it lies in the future.

decisions.choice: Asshur: most likely Assyria
alternatives: the Asshurim, a people of the Arabian desert (Genesis 25:3)
decisions.reason: Asshur is the name of Assyria, the great power of later centuries that carried whole peoples away captive (2 Kings 15:29; 17:6). Asshur is also the name of a desert people descended from Abraham (Genesis 25:3), which some think fits the Kenites' world better. The same name appears again in verse 24.

decisions.choice: Assyria
decisions.reason: Readable gives the usual English name of the nation the meaning decision prefers. Literal and Balanced keep "Asshur".

source.text: וַיִּשָּׂ֥א מְשָׁל֖וֹ וַיֹּאמַ֑ר א֕וֹי מִ֥י יִחְיֶ֖ה מִשֻּׂמ֥וֹ אֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And he lifted up his oracle and said: alas, who will live from [when] sets it God?

en.L: And he took up his oracle and said, \q "Alas, who will live when God sets this [in place]?
en.B: Then he spoke his oracle again: \q "Alas, who can survive when God does this?
en.R: Then Balaam said: \q "How terrible! Who can live through it when God does this?

decisions.choice: alas: a cry of dismay
decisions.reason: The word is a cry of grief or alarm at disaster that is coming.

decisions.choice: when God sets it: when God brings these things about
alternatives: who will live except the one God appoints?
decisions.reason: The words mean "from God's setting it", that is, when God puts these events in place. "It" most likely refers to the disasters of verses 22-24. Some take the line differently, as "who will live except the one God appoints?", but the simpler reading fits the cry of dismay.

decisions.choice: the oracle names no nation in the Hebrew
alternatives: and seeing Og, he took up his oracle (the ancient Greek translation)
decisions.reason: Unlike verses 20 and 21, this oracle does not begin with "he saw ...". The ancient Greek translation adds "and when he saw Og" at the start. The Hebrew text is followed; reviewers should check this against a textual apparatus.

decisions.choice: again
decisions.reason: Balanced adds "again", since this is one more oracle in a series of short ones.

source.text: וְצִים֙ מִיַּ֣ד כִּתִּ֔ים וְעִנּ֥וּ אַשּׁ֖וּר וְעִנּוּ־עֵ֑בֶר וְגַם־ה֖וּא עֲדֵ֥י אֹבֵֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And ships [will come] from [the] side of Kittim, and they will afflict Asshur and will afflict Eber; and also he [will come] to destruction.

en.L: And ships [will come] from the coast of Kittim, \q and they will afflict Asshur and afflict Eber; \q but he too [will come] to destruction."
en.B: Ships will come from the coast of Kittim; \q they will bring down Asshur and bring down Eber, \q but he too will perish completely."
en.R: Ships will come from the coast of Kittim. \q They will crush Assyria and Eber, \q but the attackers too will be completely destroyed."

decisions.choice: Kittim: Cyprus, then the peoples of the western sea
decisions.reason: Kittim was the name of Kition, a city on Cyprus, and then of Cyprus and the islands and coasts west of Israel (Genesis 10:4; Isaiah 23:1, 12). Later writings use it of invaders from the west across the sea, as Daniel 11:30 does. The oracle sees a seafaring power coming against the great nations of the east.

decisions.choice: Eber: peoples descended from Eber, or the lands beyond the river
decisions.reason: Eber is the ancestor of Abraham's line (Genesis 10:21-25; 11:14-26), and the name is related to the word "Hebrew". Here, beside Asshur, it may mean peoples of that descent in general, or the lands "beyond" the Euphrates, since the name also means "the other side". The oracle does not make it clear.

decisions.choice: he too will perish: the invader from the sea will fall in its turn
decisions.reason: "He" most likely refers to the power that came in ships: it brings down Asshur and Eber, but it too will come to ruin. It could also refer to Eber, the last name before it. The point either way is that every power, however great, comes to an end, as Amalek does (verse 20).

decisions.choice: afflict: humble, bring low
decisions.reason: The verb means to press down, oppress or humble. Here it is defeat in war.

decisions.choice: the attackers too
decisions.reason: Readable says who "he" is, following the grammar decision, and uses "Assyria" for Asshur as in verse 22.

source.text: וַיָּ֣קָם בִּלְעָ֔ם וַיֵּ֖לֶךְ וַיָּ֣שָׁב לִמְקֹמ֑וֹ וְגַם־בָּלָ֖ק הָלַ֥ךְ לְדַרְכּֽוֹ׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And arose Balaam and went and returned to his place, and also Balak went on his way.

en.L: And Balaam arose and went and returned to his place, and Balak also went on his way.
en.B: Then Balaam got up and went back home, and Balak also went on his way.
en.R: Then Balaam got up and went back home. Balak also went on his way.

decisions.choice: returned to his place: set off for home
decisions.reason: The phrase means that Balaam left to go home (22:5; 24:11). Numbers 31:8, 16 later finds him among the Midianites, where he advised them against Israel and was killed, so the story of Balaam does not end here.

decisions.choice: went back home
decisions.reason: "His place" means his home, as in verse 11.
